clauses.clause: Make use of texts to build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, and/or share information and ideas (any one purpose satisfies the clause — OR list). (I/C)
clauses.note: Students use the text to build knowledge — they answer comprehension questions about major events and discuss the central message, actively extracting meaning from the text to construct understanding of why the sun and moon live in the sky.

verdicts.evidence: 'What did you see and hear that helped you understand the middle of the story?' (Water came to Sun and Moon's house and brought all of his people and animals. Water filled up the house until there was no more room.)
verdicts.rationale: The standard 1.P.EICC.2.b requires students to make use of texts for any one of four interchangeable purposes (build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, share information and ideas). Students use the text "Why the Sun and the Moon Live in the Sky" to build knowledge: they answer questions about major events ("What did you see and hear that helped you understand the middle of the story?" — students respond with content drawn from the text), discuss the central message with partners ("What was the central message we learned from Why the Sun and the Moon Live in the Sky?" — "We learned that people create stories to try to explain things in nature"), role-play story events with puppets, and write responses about major events and the central message. Students also share information and ideas when cold-called to share out and when discussing with elbow partners. Multiple student-performed purposes from the OR list are evidenced, satisfying the clause fully.

clauses.note: Students refer to what they heard and saw in the text (events, illustrations) to support their answers about the beginning, middle, and end of the story, but the references are to recalled content rather than explicitly pointing to specific parts/pages/words/sentences of the text to support an idea or opinion.

verdicts.evidence: 'What did you hear that helped you understand the important events from the beginning of the story?' (Sun wants Water to visit his and Moon's house, but Water says the house is too small for all of his people. Sun and Moon decide to build a larger house.)
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to refer to parts of texts when supporting an idea, answer, or opinion. Students do answer text-based questions by recalling specific events and illustration details (e.g., "Sun wants Water to visit his and Moon's house, but Water says the house is too small for all of his people"), which constitutes referring to text content to support their answers. However, the lesson does not explicitly direct students to point to, cite, or locate specific parts of the text (pages, words, sentences, illustrations) as evidence — the references are to recalled narrative content rather than deliberate text-referencing acts. The clause is partially met because students support answers with text-derived content but the explicit "refer to parts of texts" act is narrower than the standard envisions. The turn-and-talk about why the sun and moon live in the sky and the central message also elicit text-supported answers, but again without an explicit directive to point to or cite a specific part of the text.
